name: Rejuran / salmon DNA facial

card.summary: Polynucleotide (PN) skin-booster injections made from salmon DNA, sold as a skin-quality treatment; evidence for appearance use is still thin and mostly unpublished.
card.aka: Rejuran, salmon DNA facial, PN injections, PDRN skin booster, polynucleotide skin booster
card.note: Clinic-administered injectable; public sources describe few published controlled trials, and the registered trials found are comparisons or not yet recruiting.

quick.overview:
A salmon DNA facial is a cosmetic injection treatment in which fragments of fish-derived DNA (polynucleotides, sometimes called PDRN) are placed into the skin by a clinician. Rejuran is the best-known brand. It is marketed for skin texture, fine lines, under-eye skin and general skin quality rather than for filling volume.

It entered looksmaxxing discussion as one of several injectable 'skin booster' options, grouped with other hardmaxx procedures. Registered trials exist for crow's feet and for periorbital and neck uses, but the sources found describe few published, controlled results.
quick.mechanism: Proponents and aesthetic-medicine sources say the polynucleotides stimulate fibroblast activity and collagen production and support tissue repair, and that the injection also hydrates and conditions the skin. Public encyclopedia summaries describe this as a proposed mechanism from recent studies rather than an established one.
quick.risks: Common reported effects of skin-booster injections in general are temporary redness, swelling and bruising at injection sites; as with any injection, infection and allergic reaction are possible. One general source notes that therapeutic polynucleotides can trigger immune activation. Regulation of PN products varies by country, and the sources reviewed give no skin-specific safety dataset.

lead: A Rejuran or salmon DNA facial is a cosmetic procedure in which a polynucleotide (PN) preparation, derived from salmon DNA, is injected into or just beneath the skin to improve its quality. The best-known product name is Rejuran, and the ingredient is also referred to as polydeoxyribonucleotide (PDRN). It is promoted for skin texture, fine lines, under-eye skin and overall rejuvenation rather than for adding volume the way a conventional filler does.[1]

Aesthetic-medicine descriptions say the material is thought to stimulate fibroblast activity and collagen production and to promote tissue regeneration, and report improved elasticity and reduced wrinkles after subcutaneous injection; the encyclopedia summaries do not describe the size or design of the underlying studies.[1] Wikipedia notes that fish-derived polynucleotide is used in aesthetic medicine as a dermal filler.[2]

Several clinical trials involving PN-type products have been registered, including non-inferiority and comparison studies for crow's feet lines and not-yet-recruiting studies of periorbital hollowing and horizontal neck lines.[3][4][5][6][7] In looksmaxxing communities the treatment is discussed as a skin-quality or under-eye option among injectables.

paras: Polynucleotides are chains of nucleotide units, the class of molecule that includes DNA and RNA.[2] In the aesthetic products discussed here the material is derived from salmon DNA and is described as polydeoxyribonucleotide (PDRN) or PN.[1] Preparations are delivered by a clinician as small injections into the skin, sometimes with a cannula for deeper areas, and the product category is often called a skin booster. Topical gels, creams, serums and masks containing PDRN are also sold, some using plant-based alternatives.[1]

Reviews summarised in public encyclopedias attribute the effects of PDRN to stimulation of collagen production, increased fibroblast activity and tissue regeneration, citing recent studies from 2023 to 2025; the summaries do not name a receptor pathway or describe study designs.[1]

No skin-specific adverse-event dataset is described in the public sources reviewed. A general encyclopedia entry notes that therapeutic polynucleotides can trigger immune activation, which may reduce efficacy or cause adverse effects.[1] Injection procedures in general carry risks of bruising, swelling, infection and allergic reaction.

Published controlled trials of the appearance effects of salmon-DNA injections were not found in the sources reviewed. Registered studies include a completed 2020 non-inferiority trial in 218 patients comparing an injectable (DLMR01) with a control for crow's feet lines,[3] a 2024 study of 60 patients comparing DMSB01 with Rejuran for temporary improvement of crow's feet,[4] and a 2024 trial in 171 patients of another injectable (HMM1-022) for crow's feet.[5] Two further studies, both listed as not yet recruiting, plan to evaluate a deep-plane Rejuran S technique for periorbital hollowing[6] and a dual-plane polynucleotide technique for horizontal neck lines in 30 participants each.[7] Registry entries do not report results, so the findings of these trials are not available from the listings.

Current research interest, as reflected in trial registrations, centres on periocular and neck skin and on comparing newer polynucleotide products with Rejuran.[4][6][7] Topical and plant-based PDRN alternatives are also being marketed.[1]

The treatment was added to the wiki as a hardmaxx option associated with PN injections. It is discussed by people interested in under-eye and skin-quality improvement as an injectable that aims to improve skin rather than reshape structure.

timeline.event: A non-inferiority trial of a polynucleotide-type injectable for crow's feet lines in 218 patients starts.[3]
A comparison of DMSB01 with Rejuran for crow's feet lines and a trial of HMM1-022 begin.[4][5]
Studies of Rejuran S for periorbital hollowing and PN for neck lines are registered as planned.[6][7]
